senses: Panko breaded and deep-fried Japanese food
Japanese curry, which may or may not contain a panko breaded and deep-fried food.
ety: From Japanese カツ (katsu, “cutlet”), shortening of カツレツ (katsuretsu), itself from English cutlet. Thus a doublet of English cut.
examples: Things like yakisoba and katsu curry are all examples of this western mixing, while omurice has both French and American influences. I’m 50 now and I remember growing up in the 1970s with my mother making me omurice.

senses: Any of a family of synthetic polymethine blue dyes used in photography etc.
A subsequent brief recitement or enumeration of the major points in a narrative, article, or book.
The third major section of a musical movement written in sonata form, representing thematic material that originally appeared in the exposition section.
ety: From Anglo-Norman recapitulaciun et al., Middle French recapitulacion et al., or their source, from Late Latin recapitulatio (“summing up, summary”), from the participle stem of recapitulare (“recapitulate”), from re- + capitulum (“chapter, section”), diminutive of caput (“head”).

senses: The scientific forecasting of future trends in science, technology or society
ety: From future + -ology. Attested once in 1934 as the title of play, Futureology; in later use, after German Futurologie, suggested in a 1942 letter to the American scholar John H. Herz by the German political scientist Ossip K. Flechtheim, who used futurology in a 1943 Phylon article.

senses: Synonym of quietness (“absence of sound”)
ety: Borrowed from Middle French quiétude, from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus, perfect passive participle of quiēscō (“rest”).

senses: A clenched fist.
A mathematical puzzle played on a 5 × 5 grid.
A dark brownish-grey colour, the colour of moleskin.
ety: Borrowed from French taupe, from Latin talpa (“mole”). Doublet of talpa.

senses: Body fat percentage.
onomatopoeic representation of the sound of a punch or blow.
examples: The fans thronging the theatres got the full value for the pains taken to reach there as the films were full of authentic dishoom-dishoom shots.
I'm really glad that I've moved beyond the dishoom-dishoom.

senses: Characteristic of Capri.
A piece of pottery or stone, usually broken off from a vase or other earthenware vessel, especially one used to cast a vote during the Ancient Greek process of ostracism.
The state of being sexually and romantically attracted primarily or exclusively to persons of the opposite sex.
Sexual activity with a person of the opposite sex.
A variety of zircon, ranging in color from brown, orange, reddish-brown and yellow; a jacinth.
ety: From Middle English jacinth, partly from Old French jacincte, from Medieval Latin jacintus, and partly from Old English iacinþ, from Medieval Latin jacinthus, both from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers”), ultimately from a non-Indo-European Mediterranean language. Re-Latinized in the 16th century.

senses: A fishing hook consisting of several hooks radiating from a centre.
A tool for lopping superfluous branches from a tree.
The slowest shearer in the shearing shed; an inexpert or poor shearer.
A person who reviews newly built properties to find issues to be remedied before the client buying the home moves in; someone who produces a snag list.
examples: The `ringer' looks around and is beaten by a blow. And curses the old snagger with the blue-bellied Jo.
We've gone from a small company in west Wales to the UK's number one snagger inspectors
I was a snagger on the building site, where I was going around pointing out problems.

senses: Mottled, streaked, multicoloured.
ety: From a contracted form of marble + -ed.
examples: The Standing Stones reared up above the two, marled and streaked with snow they were, and a wind came blowing fit to freeze the chilblains on a brass monkey as they stood and glowered one at the other.

senses: The depletion of surface snow and ice from a spacecraft or meteorite through melting and evaporation caused by aerodynamic heating.
ety: From Late Middle English ablacioun (“removal”), from Late Latin ablātiō (“a taking away”), from auferō (“to take away, carry off, withdraw, remove”) + -tiō (“-tion”, nominal suffix). Doublet of ablatio. Compare French ablation. By surface analysis, ablat(e) + -ion.

senses: Somebody who finds it difficult to scold or punish.
A soft drink containing no alcohol.
One who subscribes to the philosophy of cognitivism.
examples: However, the European cognitivists assimilate cognitive science into a semiotic framework, whereas the North American cognitivists work within a pure cognitive framework (one un- tainted by semiotics).

senses: A type of school in India and in several other countries, residential in nature, with pupils living near the guru, often within the same house.
To make or render toxic.
ety: Attested since 1917, apparently a back-formation from detoxify. (attested since 1905). Equivalent to tox- + -ify.
examples: The experiments made with this objective showed that agar-gel could toxify a rat serum which had been heated at 45 an 50 C. for half an hour.

senses: metal filings
ety: From Middle English lymail, from Anglo-Norman limaille, from Latin limare, a form of limo (“to file”); see further there.

senses: A sport in which snowmobiles are raced at high speed on artificial tracks.
Of ninth rank or order.
ety: From the Latin nōnārius, from nōnus (“ninth”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary).

senses: A person's dress, especially when elaborate or fine.
A person's external appearance, especially when showy.
ety: From Late Middle English plumage, plummage (“bird’s feathers collectively, plumage; (falconry) feathers fed to a hawk to cause it to regurgitate, casting”), from Middle French plumage, plomage (“bird’s feathers collectively; person’s (showy) clothing”), from Old French plumage (“bird’s feathers collectively”) (modern French plumage), from plume (“feather, plume”) + -age (suffix forming nouns denoting a state of being). senses: That has not been retouched.
examples: One of the shoes in the unretouched photograph above cost $45 a pair! The other costs just $6.60 a pair in any Regal Shoe Store!

senses: The quantity contained on a plate.
Adherence to social conventions; conventional behavior.
The doctrine that logical or mathematical principles are simply the expression of conventions.
Indications or signs.
Distinctive markings.
ety: From Latin indicia, plural of indicium (“a notice, information, discovery, sign, mark, token”), from index (“index”); see index.
examples: This document has none of the indicia of a contract of adhesion.

senses: a believer in, or advocate of, polytheism
Any aircraft that obtains its lift from rotors (usually either a helicopter or an aerial drone with rotors).
Something that is mind-bending.
examples: The ruched dresses are a mindbender, with taut stretch silk blending into draped folds.

senses: Any of several movements that promote reform
A healthcare professional who is qualified or professionally engaged in the practice of acupuncture.
A chiefly Californian ornamental evergreen shrub (Photinia arbutifolia, syn. Heteromeles arbutifolia) of the rose family having white flowers succeeded by red berries.
An inauthentic imitation of Cockney accent and vocabulary.
A person who speaks in this way.
ety: Blend of mock + Cockney. First published use in 1967, according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

senses: Biologically active; having a biological effect.
Describing a terrarium, vivarium, etc. that is self-sustaining and mimics a natural habitat.
examples: Although some cephalopod inks have been studied chemically, there’s still a lot unknown about the bioactive function of ink when released in the wild.

senses: The currency of Honduras, divided into 100 centavos.
ety: Spanish, from the name of an Indian chief.

senses: The state or property of being capable of being verified; confirmability.
examples: The issues of veracity and verifiability raised by testimony in trials emerge with a vengeance in the context of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

senses: To remove the core from.
The state of being a charlatan
An act of a charlatan
examples: It will cure by science and philosophy instead of empiricism, and will deal the deadliest blow to charlatanism.
